stories.title: Google fined €403m by data watchdog for location tracking
stories.summary: Tech giant Google has been fined €403m by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) over the processing of location data. Under data protection rules, such information must be processed in a lawful, fair and transparent manner. The DPC said that its investigation into Google found failures in this regard meaning that people could have been unaware that their location was being used to, for example, influence them with ads or to infer their interests, and could lose control over their personal data. "The retention of users' location data for longer than necessary aggravated this loss of control," said DPC Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle. "Location data is a type of personal data which is processed by way of location tracking, and includes data collected or processed by Google, which by itself or in conjunction with other information an individual's location can be inferred," Mr Doyle said. The investigation focussed on the period of May 2018 to February 2020.

stories.title: How one phone call led to report on NAS allegations
stories.summary: More than 30 women recently said they experienced sexual harassment, misogyny, bullying or intimidation while working in the National Ambulance Service (NAS). An unpublished Health Service Executive (HSE) internal review obtained by the programme also raised concerns about the culture and leadership of the service, including references to bullying and harassment and what it described as a traditional "command and control" management style. It began with one phone call. A woman wanted to speak to me about her experience working in the National Ambulance Service. During those early days looking into the culture in the service, it wasn't clear where the story would lead. But as the weeks went on, and more brave women spoke about their experience, it quickly became apparent this story was like a Russian doll with many layers. As I asked questions, one account led to another and a familiar concerning pattern began to emerge, with women independently telling similar stories.

stories.summary: Garda representative bodies and opposition politicians have called for an inquiry with the Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors, saying that they have "serious concerns around the independence of the protected disclosures process" within the garda force. The former Minister for Justice also insisted she will not consider her position at Cabinet in light of the revelations contained within the broadcast. Speaking at a Fine Gael conference for small businesses in Dublin today, Ms McEntee reiterated on a number of occasions her position from the Dáil on Thursday that she had "adhered to the law at all times" when it came to protected disclosures during her time at the Department of Justice. "That's a matter for the Minister for Justice, that's not for me to decide," said the Meath East TD when asked should there be a public inquiry into the issues. "My understanding is he's [Jim O'Callaghan] made a decision on that this morning [not to hold an inquiry] so I'm not going to cross over that," she added. On calls for urgent action to ensure the protected disclosure process within An Garda Síochána is independent, Ms McEntee again refrained from offering a viewpoint, saying it was a matter for the Minister for Justice.

stories.title: Grocery sales up 5.5% amid back to school season
stories.summary: Grocery inflation moved higher in the four weeks to September 6, new figures from Worldpanel by Numerator show today, while grocery sales rose by 5.5%. Worldpanel by Numerator reported grocery inflation of 4.28% for September, up from last month's figure of 3.87%. Worldpanel by Numerator said that value remained key for shoppers, with promotions getting one fifth of all sales. It also noted that more shoppers opted to get their shopping delivered to their front door, with home deliveries were up almost 4% year-on-year. Today's figures also show that preparation for the back to school season drove more frequent shopping trips, up 2.4% year on year. They also reveal increased volume on these trips, with an increase of 1.8%, as consumers stocked up for the new term. Irish shoppers made 44.6 million trips to supermarkets in the four weeks to September 3, an increase of 1.65 million on last month. But value remained the main priority for Irish shoppers, who spent €820m on promotional lines over the latest 12 weeks, giving a promotions value share of nearly 20.7%.

stories.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico to sue over White House ban
stories.summary: MS NOW, CNN and Politico have said they were suing the Trump Administration to protect their first amendment rights after President Donald Trump's announcement that he would ban them from the White House's building grounds. The three news outlets said they had notified the government that they were filing their lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Columbia and could see emergency hearings in the case as soon as this week, according to CNN. Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal business hours. In a social media post on friday, Mr Trump said that "other Fake News Media Outlets" would face a similar fate, but did not say which ones. A previous CNN statement called the ban "an illegal assault" on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the US government. In separate statements, MS NOW and Politico said they would "defend our first amendment rights".

stories.title: Phillips called up by Ireland after double injury setback
stories.summary: St Mirren midfielder Killian Phillips has been called up to the Republic of Ireland squad for the upcoming UEFA Nations League fixtures following a double injury blow to Heimir Hallgrimsson. Jamie McGrath (Hibernian) and Harvey Vale (Queens Park Rangers) have been forced to withdraw from the squad due to injuries sustained while on club duty over the weekend. Both players pulled up in the warm-up before games against Aberdeen and Preston North End respectively, putting their participation in doubt. Confirmation arrived this morning that they would be unavailable for the international window. Phillips will link up with the squad in Dublin today before the traveling party departs for Pristina for the match against Kosovo on Thursday. stories.title: Leitrim's Casey ready for more after faithfulness tested
stories.summary: No word of a lie, Donal Casey's life has changed utterly in the past 12 months. A year ago this weekend, the then 23-year-old was in game mode, an interested spectator in the crowd as the Leitrim SFC quarter-finals were playing out. Nothing really mattered at that time apart from a manic determination to help Leitrim Gaels, who had safely navigated a path to the semi-finals, get their hands on the Fenagh Perpetual Cup for the first time in the club’s history. Life's most valuable information in that moment was finding out who would be facing Mal Guckian’s side in the last four. He did help his club to that coveted silverware, but life isn’t just about football anymore. After what happened in that county final, his outlook changed forever. Back to that 2025 county final though and the victory over Sean O’Heslin’s. It was a day when dreams should have been realised, but for the young centre half-back, it came so close to complete tragedy.

stories.title: City overcome Sunderland despite Brobbey hat-trick
stories.summary: Brian Brobbey scored a hat-trick in a losing cause as Manchester City maintained their 100% Premier League start with a frantic 5-3 win over Sunderland. In a game characterised by poor defending, City struggled to kill off the fired-up visitors at the Etihad Stadium, with Brobbey a constant thorn in their side. Ultimately two goals from Antoine Semenyo and a late strike from Erling Haaland finished the job for City, for whom Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki were also on target. Unlike in last week's Manchester derby, City failed to assert control against a Sunderland side clearly not drained by their midweek Europa League excursions. For new manager Enzo Maresca, however, it was at least a fifth successive league win and City head into the international break with a three-point lead at the top. City were given an early warning as Sunderland broke from deep and Enzo Le Fee played in Nilson Angulo but he steered wide.

stories.title: Preview: Ireland out to keep ball rolling against USA
stories.summary: When this Ireland team made their big breakthrough at WXV1 in Canada this time two years ago, it was their phenomenal and shock win against the world champions New Zealand that made headlines. A little less notable, but just as important, was their 26-14 win against the USA in Vancouver two weeks later, which proved the Black Ferns win was no fluke, and that Scott Bemand's side were a group to watch. At the time, it was an Ireland squad still finding their feet and light on experience; current captain Erin King was in the first few games of her XVs career, Aoife Wafer was a raw talent, while Dannah O’Brien had yet to fully make the number 10 jersey her own. Of the 15 players that started against the USA two years ago, 11 will play a part this afternoon, while Clíodhna Moloney-MacDonald, Eve Higgins and O’Brien all played from the bench. In terms of personnel, there hasn’t been a great deal of change to the Ireland squad in the last couple of seasons, a sign of the age-profile in the group. However, the level of expectation around this side has changed dramatically. In the two years since that game, Ireland have cemented their place as the best of the rest in women’s rugby.

stories.title: U2 at 50: The 10 best U2 songs of all time, ranked
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. Happy Birthday, U2! One of the biggest rock bands of all time celebrates 50 years in business this month, with 15 studio albums, 12 EPs, three compilations, two live albums and no less than 85 singles released by the Dublin band over the course of that half-century. The question is, which songs are their best? It may be overplayed, it may be somewhat overcooked, it may not have the emotional heft of some of their other tracks - but only a curmudgeon would argue against Beautiful Day being one of U2’s most euphoric songs. Taken from 2001’s pivotal All That You Can’t Leave Behind album, it ushered in a new era for the band while cementing their position as one of the finest stadium rock bands on the planet. That intro alone is worth its weight in gold: the yearning squeal of The Edge’s guitar, the piano riff, the tremulous bassline, that primitive yowl of Bono’s…. 43 years after it was first released, New Year’s Day sounds as fresh as ever. The first track from U2’s third album War also incorporated social and political themes, written about the revolutionary Polish solidarity movement in 1980 which eventually led to the collapse of communism in Poland. Apparently it was originally intended as a love song about Ali Hewson. No harm, no foul, Ali. U2 have always looked to the wider world for inspiration, but this song - also taken from War - brought them closer to home and is perhaps their most explicitly political song to date. Written about the Troubles and specifically the Bloody Sunday atrocity of 1972, it’s a protest song about the futility of war, wrapped up in a spiky rock tune. From Larry Mullen’s martial cadence to Bono’s exasperated lyrics ("How long, how long must we sing this song?"), it still packs a mighty punch. By 1987, U2 had spent much of the decade touring extensively in America and absorbing its culture from the inside looking out. The result was The Joshua Tree - the album that many fans still consider their defining moment. The swarthy shuck of the guitar riff on this song, coupled with the gospel undertones and Bono’s preacher-like lyrics as it slips into the deep groove of Adam Clayton’s bassline is simply sensational stuff.

stories.title: Andrew Scott's Elsinore wins TIFF audience award
stories.summary: Dublin actor Andrew Scott’s new film Elsinore has won the International People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival. The prize was announced on Sunday as the 51st edition of the festival came to a close. The festival’s main People’s Choice Award went to Spanish drama La Bola Negra. Scott stars as Scottish actor Ian Charleson in Elsinore, which tells the story of the acclaimed actor as he prepares to play Hamlet at London’s National Theatre while living with Aids. Charleson, best known on screen for Chariots of Fire and Gandhi, stepped into the role after Daniel Day-Lewis left the National Theatre production in 1989. Directed by Simon Stone and written by Pride screenwriter Stephen Beresford, Elsinore also stars Olivia Colman, Billie Piper, Johnny Flynn, Luke Thompson, Monica Dolan, Juliet Stevenson, Joe Locke and Peter Mullan.

stories.title: Irish designer Simone Rocha bares all at London Fashion Week
stories.summary: One of Britain’s most famous criminal courts became an unlikely setting for exposed underwear and bare skin as Irish designer Simone Rocha brought her London Fashion Week show to the Old Bailey. The Dublin-born designer, known for her heavily layered dresses, frills and floral embellishments, took a noticeably less covered-up approach to her spring/summer 2027 collection, sending models through the marble halls of London’s Central Criminal Court in sheer dresses, open leather jackets and little more than underwear. It was a departure for Rocha, whose clothes often conceal the body beneath layers of tulle, tailoring and exaggerated skirts. Speaking backstage, she said she deliberately wanted this collection to feel more vulnerable. "Sometimes I can be very layered, and I can really put clothes on top of clothes; it’s a very protective thing, and I wanted to be this slightly more vulnerable," she said. One model wore a black leather jacket with a plunging neckline that extended almost to the waist, its lapels decorated with oversized leather roses.

stories.title: School meal review includes portion size and cold options
stories.summary: The Cabinet is to discuss proposals to overhaul the free hot school meals programme after two Government-commissioned reviews revealed shortcomings in the service. Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary will outline to the Cabinet the findings of two independent studies examining food standards and student, parent and teacher experience on the School Meals Programme. Mr Calleary will seek Cabinet approval for a number of changes to the scheme, after it was discovered that roughly a fifth of all hot school meals - or around 100,000 a day - go uneaten. When accounting for absences, the proportion of uneaten meals is 11.1%. Around half a million hot school meals are delivered to primary schools across the country daily, with the scheme extended nationwide in September 2025 to benefit 3,200 schools and more than 550,000 children. However, the €300 million scheme has faced some criticism, with the Oireachtas Committee on Education hearing concerns earlier this year around the nutritional quality of meals, including the level of highly processed foods and the lack of transparency regarding production methods.

stories.title: One person still in hospital after prison overdoses
stories.summary: The Irish Prison Service said that one person from the Midlands Prison remains in hospital following a series of overdoses on Friday. It said the issue was localised within the Midlands Prison and following a targeted security operation and information campaign, no further overdoses have presented since. In a statement it said: "We continue to work with the HSE to identify the drug concerned and are engaged with An Garda Síochána to identify the source of the drug." It described the assault on two staff on Friday as "unacceptable" and said the matter has been referred to gardaí for investigation. Four prisoners were hospitalised yesterday as a result of overdoses, after drugs were dropped by drone into a prison yard, according to a source. Social Democrats TD Gary Gannon described what happened in Midlands Prison as "worrying" and that he believes it reflects "that there has been an increasing normalisation of addiction in prison".

stories.title: Housing and the cost of living highlighted during protest
stories.summary: A number of trade unions and political activists marched in Dublin, calling for action on housing and the cost of living ahead of Budget 2027. SIPTU, Unite, Fórsa, and others gathered at the Garden of Remembrance to walk to Leinster House where a rally took place. Political parties such as People Before Profit, Solidarity, Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats were among those present. "The central contradiction in Ireland today is that we have a wealthy economy but the workers who create that wealth are being priced out of a decent life," SIPTU Sector Organiser Paddy Cole said before the protest. He added: "Whether people rent or hope to buy, too much of their wages is swallowed by housing. Workers from home and abroad can have qualifications, full-time jobs and good wages, yet still be unable to leave the family home, rent a decent place to live or plan for children. "That is an abject policy failure, not a failure of the people who are trying to do all the right things. This crisis unites healthcare assistants, retail workers, civil servants, hospitality workers, construction workers, transport workers and many others. Governments respond when people organise and put them under pressure."

stories.title: Oil at 1 week low on hopes of boost to diplomacy in war
stories.summary:
Oil prices slide to 11-day low on hopes of US-Iran diplomacy, Saudi exports
Oil prices slid to their lowest in 11 days today as investors hoped for diplomatic progress on the Iran war due to this week's UN meeting, and eyed a partial recovery in shipments from Saudi Arabia. Brent crude futures and US West Texas Intermediate crude touched their lowest since September 10 earlier today. The Brent contract for November was at $101.75 a barrel at 0859 GMT, down $2.12, or 2%. The WTI October contract that is expiring tomorrow fell $1.96, or 2%, to $98.34 a barrel. The November contract stood at $94.16. Iran and the US exchanged new threats yesterday, although President Donald Trump said he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly. "It seems that a degree of risk premium is being removed from oil prices on hopes that a diplomatic path to de-escalate the US-Iran war may arrive this week," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade. Iran has conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations, Al Jazeera cited Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, as saying in an interview on Saturday.

stories.title: Merz laments vote 'disaster' as AfD surges in elections
stories.summary: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) took first place in state elections in northeastern Germany, exit polls showed, delivering the worst result for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party since 1949. "It's a disaster," Mr Merz said after the exit polls were published, but signalled that he would fight on as chancellor and continue his reform agenda after speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign. The AfD was set to win 37% in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 35.5% and far in front of Mr Merz's conservatives, who got 5.5% and barely crossed the threshold to enter the state parliament, according to exit polls on ARD public television. The result looks like delivering another first-place finish at state level in a month for the AfD party, which tops national opinion polls but which has been kept from power by the refusal of the other main parties to work with it. In another election in the capital Berlin that also took place, the far-left Linke party was on 24.5%, while Mr Merz’s conservatives were on 20%. The AfD also gained in strength in the liberal city, hitting 16%.

stories.title: Sportspeople ask ROI players to boycott Israel fixtures
stories.summary: Over 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter to the Irish senior men's national football team, urging them to "act collectively with conscience" and refuse to participate in their upcoming games against Israel. The letter penned by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group calls on players to 'seize the moment' and boycott the Israel fixtures. The letter also states the FAI, UEFA, and the government have failed the players and should never have put them in this position. However, they feel that there is still time for the FAI and the government to act by refusing to participate in the two games against Israel. Among the sportspeople to have openly signed the letter are rugby stars Tony Ward - who boycotted Irish rugby tour of South Africa - and Lynne Cantwell; Olympian Ciara Mageean, former soccer international Louise Quinn, boxers Tyrone McKenna and Eric Donovan, and GAA personalities Padraig O'Hora, Joe Brolly, Colm O’Rourke, Michael Darragh Macauley, Philly McMahon, Valerie Mulcahy and Rena Buckley. Para athlete Alan Dineen and ultimate frisbee's Stephen Jones have also put their name forward, having both boycotted respective fixtures against Israel earlier this year.

stories.title: Dunne doubts there's appetite for more GAA rule changes
stories.summary: Former Offaly forward Nigel Dunne has questioned whether there is a sufficient appetite amongst the GAA public for further rule changes in Gaelic football. Several tweaks will be trialled over the coming months in third level Ryan Cup fixtures, following research and discussion amongst members of the Expert Advisory Group, which is chaired by former Mayo player and manager Kevin McStay. The EAG - which was formed following the work of the Football Review Committee - is charged with monitoring trends in the game and has come up with a number of proposals to be introduced in the coming months. Among the key proposals is the banning of fisted points (unless the ball is already in flight), limiting the number of consecutive handpasses to three and awarding four points for a goal. A backcourt rule, whereby the ball cannot return back over the halfway line, and a modified kickout rule, where the ball is no longer required to travel beyond the two-point arc, are also included in the slate of changes. "In isolation they're fine and I don’t disagree with them but the problem is why change now?

stories.title: Celtic slump continues in derby defeat to Rangers
stories.summary: Rangers racked up a second win over Celtic in eight days as boos rung around an all-green Parkhead following a 1-0 defeat by the Light Blues. Celtic's 74-year-old boss Martin O’Neill went into the game under the spotlight after two successive losses, including a bruising 3-0 Premier Sports Cup clash with the Gers at Ibrox last Sunday. To silence inside a stadium populated with home fans only, Gers striker Ryan Naderi opened the scoring in the 33rd minute and it was enough for another huge victory for Derek McInnes’s men who will feel they should have added to that goal after the break. It was a first William Hill Premiership defeat of the season for the home side, who are just two points ahead of their Glasgow rivals at the top of the table going into the international break with more pressure on O’Neill. Due to a ticket allocation spat between the two city rivals which saw the authorities step in, there were only Gers fans inside Ibrox last week and only Hoops supporters at Celtic Park and they suffered another torturous 90 minutes. In a frenetic start, Gers winger Djeidi Gassama got in behind the defence but failed to finish.

stories.title: The end of it all? Art, activism and the heroes of tomorrow
stories.summary: Led by Co-Artistic Directors Feidlim Cannon and Gary Keegan with Creative Producer Rachel Bergin, acclaimed Irish theatre company Brokentalkers have performed their work across the world. Below, they introduce their latest work Heroes Of Tomorrow, created for this year's Dublin Theatre Festival in collaboration with acclaimed theatre-maker Andy Smith. How did we get here? It feels like an increasingly fragile, slippery and constantly changing world. Wars are happening. There’s a drift to the right. Political turbulence. Things feel a bit fragile. Fragmented. You can’t quite put your finger on it. It’s like there’s a gentle rumble underneath everything. Heroes Of Tomorrow charts the life and works of celebrated Norwegian artist Jan Hansen alongside key moments of real historical resistance and rupture, including the first cave painting, the Viking invasions, the invention of written language, the suffrage movement, and that time David Hasselhoff sang in the New Year at the Brandenburg gate. How did we get here? It feels like an increasingly fragile, slippery and constantly changing world. Born in 1976 in Tromsø, Norway, Jan studied at the State Academy for Art in Oslo and then at Goldsmiths College, London, emerging onto the international art scene at the turn of the century. This was a time where the practice of relational aesthetics was all the rage. This was an art that considered change. That presented possibility. An art that focused on interactions, community and communication. An art that looked to present an alternative to the greed and trappings of a capitalist society.

stories.title: Sheeran says Gaza situation 'unjustifiable' following row
stories.summary: Ed Sheeran has said what is happening in Gaza is "catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate", as he apologised for "making mistakes" following the controversy surrounding Macklemore's removal from his tour. The English singer addressed the issue at the opening of his concert at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Saturday night, his first show since Macklemore was dropped from the US leg of his Loop Tour. Sheeran began by referring to the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, describing what happened at the Nova music festival as "horrific" and saying it had "compounded centuries of Jewish pain". "What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate," he continued. "My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and the loss of civilians' lives, of children's lives." He also said the "systemic injustice" unfolding in the West Bank "cannot be overlooked".

stories.title: OMMA founder on building a 'secret forest' cafe in wartorn Kyiv
stories.summary: Nastya Kharytonova, the Dublin-based Ukrainian founder of OMMA matcha café, speaks to Charlotte Ryan from Kyiv about endurance and inspiration, as she prepares to open the second branch of her business in the Ukrainian capital. The night after I spoke with Kharytonova about her plans to open a Kyiv branch of the café, the warehouse that had built all the dreamy, ethereal and highly specific furniture for the project was destroyed in an air attack. stories.title: Political attention set as Budget 2027 on the horizon
stories.summary: Aside from the ongoing fallout from the latest garda whistleblower revelations; political attention is now set to hone in on the Budget to be announced on Tuesday fortnight. The Coalition enters this season's edition in somewhat of a bind. Pressure is mounting that Budget 2027 not be an underwhelming one for the general public, but ongoing global uncertainty means it is impossible to know just how much must be set aside and for how long fuel supports must continue. Bilateral talks began last week in Government Buildings with Cabinet figures presenting their wish lists to Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and Minister for Finance Simon Harris. The Coalition has vowed to keep spending growth at 6% or lower in 2027 but according to those involved in the talks, that didn't stop some Government ministers presenting with lengthy scrolls of budgetary asks. One insider described the talks as a "mixed bag" with some departments coming forward with "very ambitious asks well above the 6% growth rate already agreed".

stories.title: German car workers hold protests after VW profit warning
stories.summary: German auto workers staged nationwide protests today, less than three days after a shock profit warning by Europe's biggest carmaker Volkswagen highlighted the sector's unprecedented challenges from high costs and fierce Asian rivals. The protests at Volkswagen, BMW and parts supplier Bosch come as Germany's most important industry faces painful job cuts, possible production relocations and even plant closures, a crisis that was also reflected in the result of two state elections over the weekend. Volkswagen alone plans to slash another 50,000 jobs as part of its biggest-ever turnaround agreed with stakeholders earlier this month, averting a full-blown dispute with powerful unions that still repeated calls on management to fix the issues. Volkswagen works council chief Daniela Cavallo and IG Metall union head Christiane Benner called for stronger protection against unfair competition from China, a more effective European Union subsidy policy, and the continuation of a phased retirement programme. "We expect corporate leaders and management teams to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees and for jobs," Benner told workers at Volkswagen's headquarters in Wolfsburg. European automakers are facing increased competition from Asian rivals abroad and at home, creating a major problem for Volkswagen, which is already battling overcapacity on the continent, US tariffs and plunging profits in China.

stories.title: Iran and US trade threats amid escalation of regional war
stories.summary: Iran and the United States exchanged new threats, with US President Donald Trump warning Iran would fail economically or face its leadership being wiped out if it did not make a deal, and the Iranian military saying it would retaliate harshly to any fresh attack. The conflict has looked stalemated for months, with no sign either side was ready for concessions even as it has deepened a global energy crisis, cratered swathes of Iran's economy and spilled over into new regional escalations. In a phone call with a Fox News reporter, Mr Trump said Iran's leaders should make a deal, rot economically or be wiped out, the reporter said. However, with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly, Mr Trump said he would be open to meeting him, the Fox reporter added. Mr Trump has repeatedly made vague threats of major military escalations during the conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on 28 February, without carrying them out. stories.title: USA defeat doesn't dampen debut feeling for Adams Verling
stories.summary: A 40-36 defeat to the USA means it won't go down as a dream debut for Ireland’s latest international Jemima Adams Verling, but the Connacht back row insists her first cap is still "the most incredible experience" of her life. The 20-year-old played 50 minutes on debut at Tallaght Stadium yesterday and looked at home in Test rugby, logging a whopping 16 tackles in just 50 minutes on the pitch. Ireland were 31-12 in front and seemingly cruising against Jack Hanratty’s side when Adams Verling was replaced by Brittany Hogan with 30 minutes to play. But even the second half collapse did little to quench her enthusiasm as she reflected on her first cap. "It's always unfortunate to come out with a loss at the back of the game but it was just the most incredible experience of my life and I've just so much pride for the girls," Adams Verling said. "They put their hearts out there and the intent I saw from all of them, even when I came off, they were absolutely impeccable.
